questions.question:
**In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and click the option corresponding to it. If the sentence is free from error, click the "No error" option.**

Mr. Mukesh Bhatnagar our (1)/ colleague he will attend (2)/ the meeting on our behalf. (3)/ No Error (4)
questions.solution: The error lies in the second part of the given sentence as the pronoun ‘he’ is redundant because the proper noun has already been mentioned.

questions.question:
**In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and click the option corresponding to it. If the sentence is free from error, click the "No error" option.**

As soon as I will reach (1)/ Delhi I will send you (2)/ the books you have asked for. (3)/ No Error (4)
questions.solution: The error lies in the first part of the given sentence as we do not use *will* with *as soon as* when speaking about the future. So the given sentence should read as follows: *As soon as I reach Delhi, I will send you the books you have asked for.*

questions.question:
**In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and click the option corresponding to it. If the sentence is free from error, click the "No error" option.**

As I see it, he appears (1)/ to be unreasonable anxious (2)/ about pleasing his wife. (3)/ No Error (4)
questions.solution: The error lies in the second part of the sentence as two adjectives (*unreasonable* and *anxious*) have been used successively which render the sentence grammatically incorrect. Therefore the adverb form of unreasonable (i.e. unreasonably) should be used which modifies the adjective ‘anxious’.

questions.question:
**In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and click the option corresponding to it. If the sentence is free from error, click the "No error" option.**

I finished my assignment before we (1)/ reached his wedding with great (2)/ difficulty because of heavy traffic. (3)/ No Error (4)
questions.solution:
The sentence indicates that the act of finishing the assignment had already finished before the concerned people reached ‘his’ wedding. Thus the **Past Perfect (****sub + had + v3 + object****)** should be used here in order to show that an action was completed at some point in the past before another action started. So the sentence should read as*: I had finished my assignment before we reached his wedding with great difficulty because of heavy traffic.*

Also note that the sentence as given conveys an inappropriate meaning indicating that the assignment was finished with great difficulty because of heavy traffic. To rectify the error the correction should be made in the first part of the sentence.

questions.question:
**In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and click the option corresponding to it. If the sentence is free from error, click the "No error" option.**

We were living (1)/ in Canada for (2)/ around eight years. (3)/ No Error (4)
questions.solution: ‘For’ indicates a time period upto the present, therefore, the usage of* were* (indicating that the action of living ended in the past) in the first part of the sentence is incorrect. The sentence should read as follows: *We have been living in Canada for around eight years.*

questions.question:
**The sentence(s) given with blanks are to be filled with an appropriate word(s). Four alternatives are suggested for each question. For each question, choose the correct alternative and click the button corresponding to it.**

_____ information the manager had was not enough.
questions.solution:
Here the correct answer is **The little.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The most appropriate word to fill in the blank is** 'the little'.**
 
• **Little **means** "limited or below average (hardly any)"**. It has a negative meaning.
 
 
• Example: The plants will grow into **little **bushes.
 
 
 
• **'A little'** means **"somewhat (though not that much)".** It has a positive meaning. It is used in context of 'some'.
 
 
• Example: A **little **awareness would have saved her life.
 
 
 
• **'The little'** means **"not much but all of that much available".**
 
 
• Example: He drank of **the little** water he had.
 
 
 
• The sentence implies that whatever information that was available to the manager was not enough.
 
• Thus,** ‘little’ **should be preceded by the definite article** ‘the’**.
 
• Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4.**

**Correct Sentence:**__ *__**The little**__ information the manager had was not enough.*

questions.question:
**The sentence(s) given with blanks are to be filled with an appropriate word(s). Four alternatives are suggested for each question. For each question, choose the correct alternative and click the button corresponding to it.**

It is _____ that those who expect clemency from others are seldom merciful themselves.
questions.solution:
Here the correct answer is **Paradoxical.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence compares two contradictory matters stating that those who expect clemency (mercy) are not usually merciful.
 
• Such a contradiction can be called a **paradox**.
 
• **Paradoxical **- seemingly absurd or self-contradictory.
 
 
• *Example: By glorifying the acts of violence they achieve the **paradoxical **effect of making them trivial.*
 
 
 
• Thus,** option 1** is the correct answer.

**Correct Sentence:**__ *It is **__paradoxical__ **that those who expect clemency from others are seldom merciful themselves.*

* [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__***

 
• Let's have a look at the **meaning **of the other words given in options:-

 
 
• **Strange - **unusual or surprising; difficult to understand or explain.
 
• **Stupid - **having or showing a great lack of intelligence or common sense.
 
• **Repulsive - **arousing intense distaste or disgust.

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the four alternatives, choose the word which best expresses the meaning of the given word and click the button corresponding to it.**

Nugatory
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** "futile."**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• As for the given word "**nugatory**," it means **of no value or importance; trivial or insignificant. **

 
 
• **​**Example: "The judge dismissed the argument as **nugatory **and irrelevant to the case."
 
 
 
• Here are the **meanings **of all the words in the options:
 
• **Futile**: incapable of producing any useful result; pointless or ineffective.
 
 
• Example: "His efforts to change her mind were **futile**."
 
 
 
• **Rupture**: a break or tear in something, especially a part of the body.
 
 
• Example: "He suffered a **rupture **in his hamstring during the game."
 
 
 
• **Rough**: having an uneven or irregular surface; not smooth or level.
 
 
• Example: "The road was **rough **and bumpy."
 
 
 
• **Tardy**: delayed beyond the expected or proper time.
 
 
• Example: "She was **tardy **for her meeting and missed the beginning."
 
 
 
• Thus, the correct answer is **Option 1.**

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the four alternatives, choose the word which best expresses the meaning of the given word and click the button corresponding to it.**

Moribund
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** Dying.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The word similar in meaning to **Moribund **is "Dying".
 
• Let's have a look at the meaning of the words given in the question:-
 
• **Moribund**: Moribund means near death or in a dying state, lacking vitality or vigor.
 
 
• Example: The company's **moribund** sales figures indicated that it was in serious trouble and needed to make significant changes to survive.
 
 
 
• **Chaos**: Chaos means a state of complete confusion and disorder.
 
 
• For example, "The sudden storm caused **chaos **in the streets, with cars sliding and people running for shelter."
 
 
 
• **Conclusive**: Conclusive means final or decisive, serving to settle an issue or establish the truth.
 
 
• For example, "The DNA evidence was **conclusive **and proved his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt."
 
 
 
• **Virtue**: Virtue means behavior showing high moral standards, such as honesty, courage, and generosity.
 
 
• For example, "Her **virtue **and integrity made her a respected leader in the community."
 
 
 
• **Dying**: Dying means in the process of approaching death, or coming to an end.
 
 
• For example, "The old tree was **dying**, with its leaves turning brown and falling off one by one."
 
 
 
• Clearly, the word **dying** is similar in meaning to ‘**moribund**’.
 
• Hence, **option 4 **is correct.

questions.question:
**Below are three alternatives which may be used to improve the sentence by replacing the words given in the brackets. You may choose option 1, 2 or 3. In case no improvement is needed, choose 4.**

Since 2009, there (is) no cyclone there.
questions.solution: Here the usage of since describes an action which began at a particular point of time in the past and has continued till now. Thus present perfect **(****sub + has/have + v3 + object)** form of verb should be used to make the sentence grammatically correct: *Since 2009, there has been no cyclone there.*

questions.question:
**Below are three alternatives which may be used to improve the sentence by replacing the words given in the brackets. You may choose option 1, 2 or 3. In case no improvement is needed, choose 4.**

Nisha probably (would have catching) up the bus by now.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **must have caught**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the given sentence, the phrase "would have catching" is grammatically incorrect.
 
• The appropriate phrasing should be "must have caught" to indicate a probable action completed by now.
 
• The construction "must have caught" correctly uses the modal verb **"must" **to indicate a high degree of certainty about a past action.
 
• Therefore, the correct phrase should be "must have caught" instead of "would have catching".

Hence, the correct answer is option 1.

Correct sentence: *Nisha probably **must have caught** up the bus by now*.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Modal verbs such as **"must have"**, **"should have"**, and **"could have"** are commonly used to indicate probability, obligation, or past ability with certainty regarding completed actions.
 
• These constructions follow the pattern: *Modal verb + have + past participle*.
 
 
• **Example:** *She **must have finished** her homework by now.*

questions.question: Our constitution is named _____, because
questions.solution: The first sentence states that our constitution is in the hands of many. This kind of system is known as ‘democracy’.

questions.question: it is in the hands not of the _____ but of the many.
questions.solution: The usage of ‘but’ indicates that the constitution is in the hands of many people and not in those of ‘few’. The word ‘people’ is implicit here and since it is a countable noun, ‘few’ is the most appropriate word for it.

questions.question: But our laws secure equal _____ for all their
questions.solution: A ‘remuneration’ refers to money paid for work or a service and is inappropriate in the given context which talks about the nature of ‘law’ of our country. Laws do not ensure ‘rights’, constitution does. But laws do ensure ‘justice’, therefore option 2 is the best fit answer. ‘Power’ irrelevant in the given context.

questions.question: public opinion welcomes and _____ talents in every branch
questions.solution: The usage of the conjunction ‘and’ indicates that the required word must be similar to ‘welcomes’. This, eliminates option 1. Among all the other options, ‘honours’ is the most appropriate. Also not that since a singular subject takes a singular verb, the word in the blank space should be singular (like ‘welcome**s**’). All other words except ‘honours’ are plural verbs.

questions.question: And as we give free play to _____ in our public life,
questions.solution: It has already been established that our constitution is named democracy and our laws secure equal justice to all. So it can be said that we give free play to **all **(and not to ‘few’ or ‘some) ’in our public life

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following is INCORRECT?
